summary: Garlic mustard is an invasive herb that ranks among the worst forest invaders in the Northeast and Midwest. It thrives on shady forest floors where few other non-native plants can survive, forming thick stands that block light, water, and nutrients from native wildflowers. The plant also releases chemicals that slow the growth of other plants, but removing it has been shown to restore greater variety to forests, including tree seedlings.
history: Garlic mustard originally comes from Europe and parts of Asia. People brought it to North America because they wanted to use it for medicine and food. The first time anyone recorded it growing wild in the United States was in 1868 on Long Island, New York. Since then, it has spread across the eastern United States and Canada, and it now grows as far west as Washington, Utah, and British Columbia.
seasons: Garlic mustard takes two years to complete its life cycle. In its first year, seeds sprout in February or early March and grow into a low rosette of dark green, kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges. During the second year, the plant grows a flower stalk with small white four-petaled flowers that appear in early April, followed by four-sided seedpods that form in May, and the plant dies by June. You can identify garlic mustard by crushing its leaves, which smell like garlic.

handling.text: Hand-pulling can stop garlic mustard from spreading if it is done before the seeds form. At least the upper half of the root must come out, which is easiest in spring when the soil is soft, and pulling needs to be repeated for up to five years because seeds can survive that long in the soil. Seeds are mainly spread by people and animals carrying them, so limiting foot traffic and soil disturbance in the forest helps prevent new infestations. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
